passages.t: A blameless man in the land of Uz
passages.happening:
‘There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job. And this man was blameless and upright, fearing God and shunning evil’ (verse 1). He has seven sons and three daughters, and great wealth: 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, 500 female donkeys and a very large number of servants. ‘Job was the greatest man of all the people of the East’ (verse 3).

His sons take turns holding feasts in their homes and invite their sisters. When the days of feasting are over, Job sends for his children to purify them, and he rises early to offer burnt offerings for each of them. He thinks, “Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts” (verse 5). ‘This was Job’s regular practice’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The book opens outside Israel's story. There is no mention of Abraham, Moses, the covenant or the land. Uz lay somewhere east of Israel. Lamentations 4:21 links it with Edom, and some scholars place it further north, toward Aram. Its exact place is unknown.

The setting feels very old. Job's wealth is counted in flocks and herds, and he acts as priest for his own household, as Noah, Abraham and Jacob did, with no temple and no law of Moses. A burnt offering was an animal wholly burned on the altar, given entirely to God.

Blameless, tam in Hebrew, does not mean sinless. It means whole, a life undivided and sound through and through. The narrator says it here, and the LORD will say it in verse 8. The reader is told from the first line that what follows is not a punishment.

Notice Job's care for his children. He is not anxious about anything they have done that he knows of. He covers even what may be hidden in their hearts.
passages.later: Ezekiel remembers Job, with Noah and Daniel, as one of the righteous men of old. If a land turned against God, even those three ‘could deliver only themselves’ (Ezekiel 14:14).
passages.asks: Job prayed for his children early in the morning, for things he could not see. Ask whom you carry before God in the same way. And ask what it would mean for your own life to be whole, not perfect, but undivided.

passages.t: Does Job fear God for nothing?
passages.happening:
‘One day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came with them’ (verse 6). The LORD asks where he has come from. “From roaming through the earth,” he replies, “and walking back and forth in it” (verse 7).

The LORD points to Job: “Have you considered My servant Job? For there is no one on earth like him, a man who is blameless and upright, who fears God and shuns evil” (verse 8).

Satan answers with a question: “Does Job fear God for nothing?” (verse 9). God has put a hedge around Job and all he owns and made his work prosper. “But stretch out Your hand and strike all that he has, and he will surely curse You to Your face” (verse 11).

The LORD gives him leave, with a limit: “Everything he has is in your hands, but you must not lay a hand on the man himself” (verse 12). ‘Then Satan went out from the presence of the LORD’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The scene draws on the old picture of God as a king surrounded by his council. The sons of God are heavenly beings who serve him. Among them comes ha-satan, the satan, a Hebrew word meaning the adversary or accuser, with the definite article, more like a title than a name.

The question of verse 9 turns on one word, chinnam, for nothing. Is Job's faith real, or is it paid for? If it is a transaction, it will collapse when the payments stop. That question is the hinge of the whole book.

Two things stand side by side. The accuser, not God, proposes the test and will carry it out. But he can act only with the LORD's permission and within the limit the LORD sets. The book does not hide the second fact to protect the first.

The reader now knows something Job will never be told. That gap, between what the reader knows and what Job knows, drives every chapter that follows.
passages.later: Israel knew the picture of God's council: ‘I saw the LORD sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him on His right and on His left’ (1 Kings 22:19). And the prophet Zechariah saw the accuser again, ‘with Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him’ (Zechariah 3:1).
passages.hard:
Who is the accuser, and why would God allow him to test Job?

This is one of the hardest scenes in Scripture. Readers differ on who the accuser is. Some scholars hold that he is a member of the heavenly court whose role is to test and accuse, something like a prosecutor, not yet the fully developed figure of the devil. They note the definite article, the satan, and that the same word is used elsewhere of human adversaries (1 Samuel 29:4). Most Christian interpreters, following the New Testament's picture of the accuser, identify him with Satan, the enemy of God. Either way, he is under God's authority, and he acts with hostile intent toward Job. These notes take no side.

Readers also differ on how literally to take the conversation in heaven. Some see a real glimpse into God's council. Others see a dramatic device, told in the style of a story, that sets up the book's question.

On the harder question, why God would allow it, the book gives the reader one reason and withholds the rest. It shows that the test was about whether faith can hold on to God for God's own sake. It does not claim that this scene explains every human loss. It explains Job's, and it tells the reader that there may be reasons hidden from the one who suffers. No one may take this scene and say of a grieving person that God is testing them, or that they are failing a test.
passages.asks: The accuser assumed that faith is a bargain. Ask what you love God for: what he gives, or who he is. And ask whether there is anyone whose suffering you have explained to yourself, when the book says the reasons may be hidden.

passages.t: Four messengers, and a man who worships
passages.happening:
One day, while Job's sons and daughters are eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house, a messenger comes. The Sabeans have taken the oxen and donkeys and killed the servants, “and I alone have escaped to tell you!” (verse 15).

‘While he was still speaking, another messenger came’ (verse 16). Fire has fallen from heaven and burned up the sheep and the servants. A third: the Chaldeans have raided the camels and killed the servants. A fourth: a mighty wind from the desert has struck the house where Job's children were feasting. “It collapsed on the young people and they are dead, and I alone have escaped to tell you!” (verse 19).

‘Then Job stood up, tore his robe, and shaved his head. He fell to the ground and worshiped’ (verse 20). He says, “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I will return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD” (verse 21).

‘In all this, Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The story is told in a pattern, four messengers, each arriving while the last is still speaking, each ending with the same words. Raiders, then fire, then raiders, then wind: human hands and natural forces, sweeping every part of Job's life in a single day.

The Sabeans were probably Arabian people connected with Sheba, whose raiding parties ranged widely. The Chaldeans here are best understood as tribal raiders from southern Mesopotamia, before the Chaldean kings who later ruled Babylon.

Tearing the robe, shaving the head and falling to the ground were the familiar signs of grief across the ancient world. Job does all of them. His worship does not replace his mourning. It happens inside it.

The book tells the death of the children in two verses and does not linger, and neither will these notes. What matters for the book is that Job's grief and his worship stand together, and that the narrator says he did not sin.
passages.later: The New Testament remembers how it ended: ‘You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy’ (James 5:11).
passages.hard:
Ten children die in one day. What does the book say about that, and what does it not say?

The book does not explain the deaths to Job, and it does not make them smaller. Job tears his robe and falls to the ground. In chapter 3 he will curse the day he was born. His worship in verse 21 is real, and so is the anguish that follows; the book holds both, and readers who have lost a child need not choose between them.

The book also does not say that Job's children died for anything they did. Job's worry about their hearts in verse 5 is a father's care, not the cause of their deaths. And at the end of the book, when Job has seven sons and three daughters again, the text does not pretend that new children replace the ones who died. No child replaces another.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Job worshiped on the day he lost everything, and he grieved for many days after. Ask whether you have let yourself do both. And if someone near you is grieving, ask how you might sit with them before you say anything at all.
